**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

after.quote:
Fix an input dimension $n\ge0$, finitely many operation nodes $1,\ldots,T$, and a designated output node $o$, either an input coordinate or an operation, whose value space is $\mathbb R$. Input coordinate $i$ has value $x_i$ and value space $\mathbb R$ with its standard Euclidean inner product. Operation node $j$ has an ordered list of parent slots $p_{j,1},\ldots,p_{j,r_j}$; each slot points to an input or an operation with index less than $j$. Repeated parent slots are allowed and count separately. The graph is a finite straight-line program because every operation reads only earlier values and there are no data-dependent loops.

For each operation $j$, choose a dimension $d_j\ge0$, set $E_j=\mathbb R^{d_j}$ with its standard Euclidean inner product, take an open set $U_j\subseteq E_{p_{j,1}}\times\cdots\times E_{p_{j,r_j}}$ with the product inner product, and choose a primitive map $\phi_j:U_j\to E_j$. A smooth primitive is $C^1$: it is totally differentiable and its derivative matrix is continuous. For Hessian-vector products require the primitive to be $C^2$, meaning $C^1$ with a continuously differentiable derivative map. Derivatives are represented in these coordinates, and every transpose is the Euclidean transpose for the stated inner products; the gradient of a scalar output is the Euclidean gradient. The real-arithmetic primal recursion is $z_j=\phi_j(z_{p_{j,1}},\ldots,z_{p_{j,r_j}})$ whenever the parent tuple lies in $U_j$. Its admissible input domain is the set of $x\in\mathbb R^n$ for which every operation in this recursion is defined. The graph's scalar output function $f$ is the value at $o$: it is $x_i$ when $o$ is input coordinate $i$, and $z_j$ when $o$ is operation node $j$.

The **primal tape** is the finite ordered record of input and node values, parent-slot indices, primitive identities, and (when applicable) selected branch labels. A deterministic replay starts from the identical checkpoint state and applies the identical primitive maps in the identical order, so it reproduces the same real-arithmetic values and local derivative inputs. Opaque solver calls are not primitive operations unless their complete deterministic map and derivative rule are explicitly supplied.

A piecewise-$C^1$ primitive is specified by finitely many open branch regions and a $C^1$ formula on each region; its primal boundary value, if any, is specified separately. If the current parent tuple lies strictly inside exactly one declared branch, the program uses that branch and its derivative. At a branch boundary or ambiguous branch selection, forward or reverse AD returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE; it does not silently choose a subgradient or generalized derivative. If no primal value is specified at a boundary, that input is outside the program's domain. All correctness theorems below apply on a fixed strict branch. The same convention applies to piecewise-$C^2$ primitives for Hessian-vector products.

Let $f:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be the output of a finite $C^1$ program on a fixed strict branch. For every admissible $x\in\Omega$ and direction $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the forward-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)v$.

For a finite $C^1$ program with one scalar output $f$, on a fixed strict branch and at every admissible $x$, the reverse-mode algorithm returns $Df(x)^T1$, the gradient of $f$. More precisely, at any operation node $i$, if its value is temporarily treated as an independent variable and all later operations are recomputed from it, then the accumulated cotangent at $i$ is the derivative of the scalar output with respect to that independent node value.

Let $R:\Theta\times Z\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, where $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open. Suppose $R(\theta_0,z_0)=0$ and the state Jacobian $R_z(\theta_0,z_0)$ is invertible. The Euclidean implicit function theorem gives a local $C^1$ solution branch $z=\phi(\theta)$, and
$$D\phi(\theta_0)=-R_z(\theta_0,z_0)^{-1}R_\theta(\theta_0,z_0).$$
For a scalar $C^1$ objective $J(\theta,z)$, its derivative along that branch is
$$D(J(\theta,\phi(\theta)))|_{\theta_0}=J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta.$$
Equivalently, if $\lambda$ solves $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$, this derivative is $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$. These formulas concern the exact local solution branch; differentiating a stopped iteration is a separate finite-map derivative.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

**A floating-point system.** A floating-point system consists of a nonempty
finite set $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb R$ of representable numbers with
$0\in\mathbb F$ and $-\mathbb F=\mathbb F$, a positive real
$N_{\max}\in\mathbb F$ (the largest normal magnitude), a positive real
$N_{\min}\in\mathbb F$ (the smallest normal magnitude), with
$N_{\min}\le N_{\max}$, and a rounding map
$\operatorname{fl}$ defined on $0$ and on the real numbers $t$ with
$N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$, taking values in $\mathbb F$ and satisfying
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$.

**Unit roundoff.** A real $u>0$ is a **unit roundoff** for the system when
every real $t$ with $N_{\min}\le|t|\le N_{\max}$ satisfies

$$\operatorname{fl}(t)=t(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u,$$

with $|\cdot|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). The model quantifies all
subsequent error analysis through the single constant $u$ and says nothing
about the internal bit representation beyond the bound $|\delta|\le u$.

**The standard relative model.** For each operation
$\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$ and all $x,y\in\mathbb F$ such that $x\circ y$ is
zero or is a real number in the normal range
($N_{\min}\le|x\circ y|\le N_{\max}$; for $\div$ this includes $y\ne 0$), the
computed result is

$$\operatorname{fl}(x\circ y)=(x\circ y)(1+\delta)\qquad\text{for some }\delta\text{ with }|\delta|\le u.$$

When $x\circ y=0$, this identity is the exact-zero rule
$\operatorname{fl}(0)=0$ and one may take $\delta=0$.

**The exclusions are part of the model, and are stated explicitly.**

- **Overflow** is excluded: when $|x\circ y|>N_{\max}$ the result is not a real
  number of the form $(x\circ y)(1+\delta)$ with $|\delta|\le u$.
- **Underflow** is excluded: when $0<|x\circ y|<N_{\min}$ the result falls into
  the subnormal or lost range and need not satisfy the relative bound.
- **Invalid operations** are excluded: when $x\circ y$ is not a real number
  (for example $0/0$), there is no real $\delta$ for the displayed identity.

Every item on this page that uses the model therefore carries the hypotheses
that the relevant operations lie in the normal range, and statements about
overflow, underflow or invalid operations are made only where the exclusion is
mentioned.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let $u\ge 0$, let
$\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|\delta_i|\le u$ for every
$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

Initialize every operation cotangent to zero and set the scalar output cotangent $\bar z_o=1$. For $j=T,T-1,\ldots,1$, and for every parent slot $k=1,\ldots,r_j$, accumulate

before.claim: By [F3], the terminal linear adjoint equation has a unique $C^1$ solution on $[0,T]$.

For a parameter increment $h$, the mean-value integral formula for the $C^1$ integrand, uniform continuity on the compact tube, and [F1] show that the objective difference quotient converges uniformly in $t$ to $D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)S(t)$. The terminal difference quotient converges to $D_\theta\phi^T+D_u\phi\,S(T)$. Uniform convergence permits integrating the running derivative, so $\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T+\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$.

In [F2], set $A=D_uf$, $B=D_\theta f$, and $g=D_u\ell^T$. The adjoint equation in the Statement and tangent equation in [F1] satisfy its hypotheses. Since $p(T)=D_u\phi^T$, the identity gives $$S(T)^TD_u\phi^T-p(0)^TD_\theta u_0=\int_0^T(-D_u\ell\,S+p^TD_\theta f)\,dt.$$
Substitute step 1.3 into step 1.2; the terms involving $D_u\ell\,S$ cancel, leaving the asserted continuous adjoint gradient formula.

after.claim: By [F3], the terminal linear adjoint equation has a unique $C^1$ solution on $[0,T]$.

By [F1], the state depends $C^1$ on the parameter and has sensitivity $S$. The chain rule gives the column gradient of the running integrand as $D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+S(t)^TD_u\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T$. The mean-value integral formula, boundedness and uniform continuity of the objective derivatives on the common compact tube, and the uniform first-order state remainder from [F1] make the running first-order remainder $o(\|h\|)$ uniformly in $t$ for a parameter increment $h$. Integration therefore gives its derivative by integrating that column gradient. The terminal chain rule gives $D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T$. Consequently $\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi^T+S(T)^TD_u\phi^T+\int_0^T(D_\theta\ell^T+S^TD_u\ell^T)\,dt$.

In [F2], set $A=D_uf$, $B=D_\theta f$, and $g=D_u\ell^T$. The adjoint equation in the Statement and tangent equation in [F1] satisfy its hypotheses. Transposing that row pairing identity and using $p(T)=D_u\phi^T$ gives $$S(T)^TD_u\phi^T-D_\theta u_0^Tp(0)=\int_0^T(-S^TD_u\ell^T+D_\theta f^Tp)\,dt.$$
Substitute step 1.3 into step 1.2; the terms involving $S^TD_u\ell^T$ cancel, leaving the asserted continuous adjoint gradient formula.

Let $u_\theta$ solve the parameter-dependent ODE of [[lem-parameter-ode-flow-tangent-on-common-tube]] on $[0,T]$. Let
$$J(\theta)=\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)+\int_0^T\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)\,dt,$$
where $\phi$ and $\ell$ are $C^1$ on a neighborhood of the trajectory tube and their first derivatives are bounded and uniformly continuous there. Let $S=D_\theta u_\theta$ be the tangent from that lemma. Let $p$ solve the terminal adjoint problem
$$-p'(t)=D_u f(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^Tp(t)+D_u\ell(t,u_\theta(t),\theta)^T,\qquad p(T)=D_u\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T.$$
Then
$$\nabla_\theta J=D_\theta\phi(u_\theta(T),\theta)^T+p(0)^TD_\theta u_0(\theta)+\int_0^T\bigl(D_\theta\ell(t,u_\theta,\theta)^T+D_\theta f(t,u_\theta,\theta)^Tp(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$
This formula separates initial, terminal, running-cost and vector-field parameter terms. It applies only while the common-tube and differentiability hypotheses hold.
